prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology and peptide biology of GLP-1 that established the incretin principle and enabled GLP-1-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings place B028 first, but I would not count that as merit. The case is the discovery chain itself: proglucagon processing, identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, its glucose-dependent insulinotropic action and its central and gastric effects, followed by a therapeutic class whose benefit in diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal outcomes is confirmed by large independent trials. The discovery changed both the field and clinical practice, and its maturity is not in doubt. A prize for the discovery, as opposed to a career, fits here. Drucker, Holst and Mojsov best represent the physiological and molecular discovery, which is what the citation should describe.
statement.case_against: The main reservation is attribution. Habener, a central contributor to proglucagon and GLP-1 biology, is not among the credited names. Mojsov's priority for identifying the active peptide is contested. Knudsen's work is the step that turned the biology into liraglutide and semaglutide, so a three-person physiology prize leaves out the drug-development step that produced the clinical impact. The three-person cap makes any allocation here open to criticism, and the committee should state clearly which of those two things (discovery or development) it is rewarding.

responses.point: Linnarsson prefers Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, arguing that Knudsen's translational design of the long-acting analogues made the biology a medicine, and that Mojsov's credit is real but contested.
responses.response: I take the point that without Knudsen there is no medicine. But the prize recognises a discovery, and the discovery here is hormone physiology and peptide identification. Industrial optimisation of a known peptide is a different kind of contribution. Mojsov's priority is contested, but the peptide-identification step is a scientific discovery, whereas a Knudsen seat would reward development. I would only change my view if the committee decides the citation should be about the therapy, and in that case Holst and Drucker plus Knudsen is defensible, though I would still want Habener's role dealt with.

responses.point: Svenningsson also proposes Knudsen as the drug-development representative, and ranks CAR-T (B045) second and HPV VLP vaccines (B019) third, with CAR-T attributed to June, Sadelain and Rosenberg.
responses.response: On B028 we differ only on the third name, and I accept that this cannot be resolved from the supplied text. On CAR-T I qualify his trio. Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer and TIL work is a distinct line from the engineered chimeric-receptor concept, and the credited list already omits Eshhar, who originated the chimeric receptor. Adding Rosenberg makes a trio that mixes two lines of work and leaves the gap unfilled. If CAR-T is chosen, June and Sadelain is the cleaner configuration.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks CAR-T second and splice-switching antisense therapy for SMN2 (B037, Krainer and Bennett) third, praising its compact and clearly complementary attribution.
responses.response: I agree that B037 has clean attribution and a dramatic clinical effect, and I respect that argument. But it did not get broad support in the other openings, and the credited names omit the early SMN2 oligonucleotide work that Sandberg himself notes. For that reason I keep it below B045 and B014 for a first prize. It may well be a strong candidate in later years, and I would not exclude it from a two-part configuration.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks cGAS-STING (B051) fourth, with Chen and Barber as the cleanest pair, and notes its relevance to interferon-driven autoimmunity.
responses.response: I agree the Chen and Barber pairing is the cleanest allocation, and that genetic evidence from STING-associated disease supports the biology. My hesitation is the one she raises herself: clinical translation is unproven and credit is shared across several groups working simultaneously on cyclic dinucleotides. That makes it a strong prospect but not yet competitive with B028 or B014 in my view.

responses.point: El Manira ranks the unfolded protein response (B020) second, with a clean Walter and Mori attribution and decades of confirmation, and treats the optogenetics claim as tool development with a six-name credit problem.
responses.response: I share his view of B020: it is conceptually original and the attribution is cleaner than for any other shortlisted candidate. It is the strongest purely basic-science option and my first choice if a second part were wanted. I do disagree that the optogenetics case is weakened much by being a tool. The prize has honoured methods that opened new fields. The real difficulty with B014 is that six credible names do not fit in three places.

uncertainties: Fair allocation among Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen and the uncredited Habener cannot be resolved from the shortlist text.
Whether the committee should reward basic hormone physiology or the development of the drugs.

Whether a two-part configuration (for example GLP-1 plus UPR) would be preferable to one broad prize, since B020 has the cleaner attribution but its three-person union would exceed the cap with three GLP-1 names.
My account of the priority history is from recollection and has not been verified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate is apparent from my profile. My nuclear receptor work with Ronald Evans and my dopamine neuron research do not overlap with the shortlisted discoveries. I have co-authored with colleagues Svenningsson and El Manira, which is a collegial tie and not a recusal issue.
